title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
read_level: full (arXiv HTML v1, Secs 1-9 and all tables; math recovered from alt text; figures read from captions only)
why_wsp: Provides a sparse gradient fine-tuning baseline (AdamW on 140 to 139,750 gradient-selected weights) for the GPT-6 Astra Qwen3.5-0.8B loop-repair edit of the MIT WSP post, analyses both edits mechanistically, re-evaluates the public Astra checkpoint, and combines the two edits; no LLM editor is used.
facets: application domain: LLM math reasoning (thinking loops)
domain: LLM math reasoning; thinking-mode loop repair in Qwen3.5-0.8B
editor: none (gradient baseline: AdamW sparse fine-tuning on gradient-magnitude-selected weights); compared with the public GPT-6 Astra edit
target: Qwen3.5-0.8B (873M params, no bias terms in linear layers)
interface: other (sparse gradient fine-tuning on the model's own correct answers; plus forward hooks adding constant vectors for the mechanism test)
fraction_or_count_of_weights_changed: "Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient" (Abstract); four-column variant 4,096 weights; after bf16 rounding "1,397 of 1,398; 138,772 of 139,750; 130,188 of 131,072" values change (Sec 2). Astra edit: "64 columns of mlp.down_proj in layers 15 and 19: 131,072 weights, 0.015% of the model's 873M" (Sec 1).

headline_results.quote: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%.
raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0–45.5% after 2–9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%
At 139,750 weights, about the size of the Astra edit, even random positions work (43.4%), so an edit of that size is not small for this behaviour.
In the 1,398-weight edit, 888 weights (64%) fall in four input columns of linear_attn.out_proj in layers 0–2.

Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit.
headline_results.where: Abstract; Sec 4 Eq 1 b_L = sum_c mu_c Delta_{:,c}

headline_results.quote: base + vectors scores 45.8% with 57 answers closed; the edited model scores 42.7% (69 closed) and the base model 11.5% (1 closed). The vectors match the four-column edit's accuracy, but not all of its closing.
the mean KL divergence from the edited model is 0.010 nats per token for base + vectors, against 0.108 for the base model, and the top-1 token agrees 98.1% of the time, against 93.2%
The four channels are not the whole edit: its 510 weights outside them score higher alone (about 33%) than the 888 inside them (about 25%).
Train the four channel columns from scratch | 4,096 | 45.8% / 44.0% ... Train four random columns, same matrices | 4,096 | 20.4% / 20.6%
The fair baseline is the base model with thinking off, which scores 41.0% ... The 1,398-weight edit matches it: 41.0% ( p=1.0 ) and 44.8% ( p=0.10 ).
With thinking off, the edited models score 40.2–41.4%, the same as the base model. The edits make thinking mode usable but add little reasoning ability.
A dense LoRA (rank 16, changing 409M weights) reaches 41.0%, no better than 1,398 sparse weights.

headline_results.claim: Astra edit on this paper's 4k protocol
Astra edit reproduction under Astra protocol
headline_results.quote: Our run of the public Astra checkpoint scores 55.7% (any correct), with 32.0% of answers hitting the limit, against 51.0% and 31.6% in their re-run (Table 7). Its strict score is 52.1%.
Ours is better at every budget up to 16k; the Astra edit passes it between 16k and 32k
It scores 62.2% at 32k, 10.1 points above the Astra edit (better on 135 problems, worse on 54, p=3×10^-9 ), with 11,523 tokens per answer against 21,966.
Our half-strength edit on its own scores 46.7% and runs out of tokens 42.9% of the time, so the gain needs both edits ( p=2×10^-19 against it).

Adding our 139,750-weight edit to the Astra edit at full strength fixes the running out (0.5% hit the limit) but undoes the long thinking: the median answer falls to 1,068 tokens, and the score to 49.7%.

headline_results.claim: Edits are near-orthogonal and differ in kind
headline_results.quote: The Astra edit lives in other layers, points in a nearly orthogonal direction and depends on the input.

cost.quote: after 2–9 minutes of training on one GPU
The 50- and 500-example sets were drawn from the full pool, which took 57.6 A100-minutes to generate
The whole project, including unrelated and failed runs, used about $49 of cloud compute: about $30 for the main study and $19 for the Astra-protocol runs.

baselines_and_controls: Base thinking-on and thinking-off (greedy); random-position sparse edits (1,398 and 139,750); dense LoRA rank 16; four random columns; part-wise ablations of the 1,398 edit; constant-vector hooks; public Astra checkpoint under both protocols; Astra + ours at strengths 1, 0.5, 0.25; transfer to GSM8K, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench v6.
runs_and_variance: "Thinking-on results use two seeds, and dense LoRA and the 13,975-weight edit were each trained once." Exact McNemar or sign tests on paired problems; two samples per problem under Astra protocol (Astra used four).
robustness_of_edits: Transfer to GSM8K (13.6% to 56.1% at 4k) but not code (HumanEval thinking-off 34.1% to 29.3%, n.s.); results across token budgets 2k-32k. Not tested under quantization or further fine-tuning.
verification: none formal; statistical tests (McNemar, sign test)
memorization_vs_reasoning: n/a (no LLM editor). Mechanistic note: 'One plausible reading: the Astra edit improves how the model reasons, and a weakened version of our constant push makes it stop once it is done.'
limitations_stated: One model only; no models with bias terms tested; two seeds; combination strength chosen on MATH-500 itself from three values with no held-out set ('the 62.2% figure is the best of three'); bias test only for the four-column edit on 38 traces and 96 problems with a different inference engine; parts outside the four channels not tested as constant vectors; random positions tested only at two sizes; may slightly hurt code.
code_or_data: none found (paper links the public Astra checkpoint https://huggingface.co/RikiyaT/Qwen3.5-0.8B-weight-space-programming)
cites_or_builds_on: Takehi et al. 2026 Sparks of Weight-Space Programming blog [1] and HF checkpoint [2]
Hu et al. Exploring weight-space programming, arXiv:2611.09382 [3]
notes_for_survey: Gradient baseline for the MIT Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 edit: at 4k tokens a 140-1,398-weight gradient edit reaches the base model's own thinking-off score, so that gain is absorbed by simply disabling thinking; its core acts as a constant residual vector (bias) through near-constant channels in layers 0-2, but only the four-column part was tested as such and the non-channel part scores higher alone. Under the 32k Astra protocol the Astra edit beats the gradient edits (52.1% vs 45.6-45.7%), and adding the gradient edit at half strength to it gives 62.2%, with the strength picked on the test set.
